title: Inside OpenAI’s in-house data agent
content:
Data powers how systems learn, products evolve, and how companies make choices. But getting answers quickly, correctly, and with the right context is often harder than it should be. To make this easier as OpenAI scales, we built our own bespoke in-house AI data agent that explores and reasons over our own platform.
Our agent is a custom internal-only tool (not an external offering), built specifically around OpenAI’s data, permissions, and workflows. We’re showing how we built and use it to help surface examples of the real, impactful ways AI can support day-to-day work across our teams. The OpenAI tools we used to build and run it (Codex, our GPT‑5 flagship model, the Evals API(opens in a new window), and the Embeddings API(opens in a new window)) are the same tools we make available to developers everywhere.
Our data agent lets employees go from question to insight in minutes, not days. This lowers the bar to pulling data and nuanced analysis across all functions, not just by our data team. Today, teams across Engineering, Data Science, Go-To-Market, Finance, and Research at OpenAI lean on the agent to answer high-impact data questions. For example, it can help answer how to evaluate launches and understand business health, all through the intuitive format of natural language. The agent combines Codex-powered table-level knowledge with product and organizational context. Its continuously learning memory system means it also improves with every turn.
In this post, we’ll break down why we needed a bespoke AI data agent, what makes its code-enriched data context and self-learning so useful, and lessons we learned along the way.
OpenAI’s data platform serves more than 3.5k internal users working across Engineering, Product, and Research, spanning over 600 petabytes of data across 70k datasets. At that size, simply finding the right table can be one of the most time-consuming parts of doing analysis.
As one internal user put it:
“We have a lot of tables that are fairly similar, and I spend tons of time trying to figure out how they’re different and which to use. Some include logged-out users, some don’t. Some have overlapping fields; it’s hard to tell what is what.”
Even with the correct tables selected, producing correct results can be challenging. Analysts must reason about table data and table relationships to ensure transformations and filters are applied correctly. Common failure modes—many-to-many joins, filter pushdown errors, and unhandled nulls—can silently invalidate results. At OpenAI’s scale, analysts should not have to sink time into debugging SQL semantics or query performance: their focus should be on defining metrics, validating assumptions, and making data-driven decisions.
Let’s walk through what our agent is, how it curates context, and how it keeps self-improving.
Our agent is powered by GPT‑5.2 and is designed to reason over OpenAI’s data platform. It’s available wherever employees already work: as a Slack agent, through a web interface, inside IDEs, in the Codex CLI via MCP(opens in a new window), and directly in OpenAI’s internal ChatGPT app through a MCP connector(opens in a new window).
Users can ask complex, open-ended questions which would typically require multiple rounds of manual exploration. Take this example prompt, which uses a test data set: “For NYC taxi trips, which pickup-to-dropoff ZIP pairs are the most unreliable, with the largest gap between typical and worst-case travel times, and when does that variability occur?”
The agent handles the analysis end-to-end, from understanding the question to exploring the data, running queries, and synthesizing findings.
One of the agent’s superpowers is how it reasons through problems. Rather than following a fixed script, the agent evaluates its own progress. If an intermediate result looks wrong (e.g., if it has zero rows due to an incorrect join or filter), the agent investigates what went wrong, adjusts its approach, and tries again. Throughout this process, it retains full context, and carries learnings forward between steps. This closed-loop, self-learning process shifts iteration from the user into the agent itself, enabling faster results and consistently higher-quality analyses than manual workflows.
The agent covers the full analytics workflow: discovering data, running SQL, and publishing notebooks and reports. It understands internal company knowledge, can web search for external information, and improves over time through learned usage and memory.
High-quality answers depend on rich, accurate context. Without context, even strong models can produce wrong results, such as vastly misestimating user counts or misinterpreting internal terminology.
To avoid these failure modes, the agent is built around multiple layers of context that ground it in OpenAI’s data and institutional knowledge.
- Metadata grounding: The agent relies on schema metadata (column names and data types) to inform SQL writing and uses table lineage (e.g., upstream and downstream table relationships) to provide context on how different tables relate.
- Query inference: Ingesting historical queries helps the agent understand how to write its own queries and which tables are typically joined together.
- Curated descriptions of tables and columns provided by domain experts, capturing intent, semantics, business meaning, and known caveats that are not easily inferred from schemas or past queries.
Metadata alone isn’t enough. To really tell tables apart, you need to understand how they were created and where they originate.
- By deriving a code-level definition of a table, the agent builds a deeper understanding of what the data actually contains. 
  - Nuances on what is stored in the table and how it is derived from an analytics event provides extra information. For example, it can give context on the uniqueness of values, how often the table data is updated, the scope of the data (e.g., if the table excludes certain fields, it has this level of granularity), etc.
- This provides enhanced usage context by showing how the table is used beyond SQL in Spark, Python, and other data systems.
- This means that the agent can distinguish between tables that look similar but differ in critical ways. For example, it can tell whether a table only includes first-party ChatGPT traffic. This context is also refreshed automatically, so it stays up to date without manual maintenance.
- The agent can access Slack, Google Docs, and Notion, which capture critical company context such as launches, reliability incidents, internal codenames and tools, and the canonical definitions and computation logic for key metrics.
- These documents are ingested, embedded, and stored with metadata and permissions. A retrieval service handles access control and caching at runtime, enabling the agent to efficiently and safely pull in this information.
- When the agent is given corrections or discovers nuances about certain data questions, it's able to save these learnings for next time, allowing it to constantly improve with its users. 
  - As a result, future answers begin from a more accurate baseline rather than repeatedly encountering the same issues.
  - The goal of memory is to retain and reuse non-obvious corrections, filters, and constraints that are critical for data correctness but difficult to infer from the other layers alone.
  - For example, in one case, the agent didn’t know how to filter for a particular analytics experiment (it relied on matching against a specific string defined in an experiment gate). Memory was crucially important here to ensure it was able to filter correctly, instead of fuzzily trying to string match.
- When you give the agent a correction or when it finds a learning from your conversation, it will prompt you to save that memory for next time. 
  - Memories can also be manually created and edited by users.
  - Memories are scoped at the global and personal level, and the agent’s tooling makes it easy to edit them.
- When no prior context exists for a table or when existing information is stale, the agent can issue live queries to the data warehouse to inspect and query the table directly. This allows it to validate schemas, understand the data in real-time, and respond accordingly.
- The agent is also able to talk to other Data Platform systems (metadata service, Airflow, Spark) as needed to get broader data context that exists outside the warehouse.
We run a daily offline pipeline that aggregates table usage, human annotations, and Codex-derived enrichment into a single, normalized representation. This enriched context is then converted into embeddings using the OpenAI embeddings API(opens in a new window) and stored for retrieval. At query time, the agent pulls only the most relevant embedded context via retrieval-augmented generation(opens in a new window) (RAG) instead of scanning raw metadata or logs. This makes table understanding fast and scalable, even across tens of thousands of tables, while keeping runtime latency predictable and low. Runtime queries are issued to our data warehouse live as needed.
Together, these layers ensure the agent’s reasoning is grounded in OpenAI’s data, code, and institutional knowledge, dramatically reducing errors and improving answer quality.
One-shot answers work when the problem is clear, but most questions aren’t. More often, arriving at the correct result requires back-and-forth refinement and some course correction.
The agent is built to behave like a teammate you can reason with. It’s a conversational, always-on and handles both quick answers and iterative exploration.
It carries over complete context across turns, so users can ask follow-up questions, adjust their intent, or change direction without restating everything. If the agent starts heading down the wrong path, users can interrupt mid-analysis and redirect it, just like working with a human collaborator who listens instead of plowing ahead.
When instructions are unclear or incomplete, the agent proactively asks clarifying questions. If no response is provided, it applies sensible defaults to make progress. For example, if a user asks about business growth with no date range specified, it may assume the last seven or 30 days. These priors allow it to stay responsive and non-blocking while still converging on the right outcome.
The result is an agent that works well both when you know exactly what you want (e.g., “Tell me about this table”) and just as strong when you’re exploring (e.g., “I’m seeing a dip here, can we break this down by customer type and timeframe?”).
After rollout, we observed that users frequently ran the same analyses for routine repetitive work. To expedite this, the agent's workflows package recurring analyses into reusable instruction sets. Examples include workflows for weekly business reports and table validations. By encoding context and best practices once, workflows streamline repeat analyses and ensure consistent results across users.
Building an always-on, evolving agent means quality can drift just as easily as it can improve. Without a tight feedback loop, regressions are inevitable and invisible. The only way to scale capability without breaking trust is through systematic evaluation.
In this section, we’ll discuss how we leverage OpenAI’s Evals API(opens in a new window) to measure and protect the agent’s response quality.
Its Evals are built on curated sets of question-answer pairs. Each question targets an important metric or analytical pattern we care deeply about getting right, paired with a manually authored “golden” SQL query that produces the expected result. For each eval, we send the natural language question to its query-generation endpoint, execute the generated SQL, and compare the output against the result of the expected SQL.
Evaluation doesn’t rely on naive string matching. Generated SQL can differ syntactically while still being correct, and result sets may include extra columns that don’t materially affect the answer. To account for this, we compare both the SQL and the resulting data, and feed these signals into OpenAI’s Evals grader. The grader produces a final score along with an explanation, capturing both correctness and acceptable variation.
These evals are like unit tests that run continuously during development to identify regressions as canaries in production; this allows us to catch issues early and confidently iterate as the agent's capabilities expand.
Our agent plugs directly into OpenAI’s existing security and access-control model. It operates purely as an interface layer, inheriting and enforcing the same permissions and guardrails that govern OpenAI’s data.
All of the agent’s access is strictly pass-through, meaning users can only query tables they already have permission to access. When access is missing, it flags this or falls back to alternative datasets the user is authorized to use.
Finally, it's built for transparency. Like any system, it can make mistakes. It exposes its reasoning process by summarizing assumptions and execution steps alongside each answer. When queries are executed, it links directly to the underlying results, allowing users to inspect raw data and verify every step of the analysis.
Building our agent from scratch surfaced practical lessons about how agents behave, where they struggle, and what actually makes them reliable at scale.
Early on, we exposed our full tool set to the agent, and quickly ran into problems with overlapping functionality. While this redundancy can be helpful for specific custom cases and is more obvious to a human when manually invoking, it’s confusing to agents. To reduce ambiguity and improve reliability, we restricted and consolidated certain tool calls.
We also discovered that highly prescriptive prompting degraded results. While many questions share a general analytical shape, the details vary enough that rigid instructions often pushed the agent down incorrect paths. By shifting to higher-level guidance and relying on GPT‑5’s reasoning to choose the appropriate execution path, the agent became more robust and produced better results.
Schemas and query history describe a table’s shape and usage, but its true meaning lives in the code that produces it. Pipeline logic captures assumptions, freshness guarantees, and business intent that never surface in SQL or metadata. By crawling the codebase with Codex, our agent understands how datasets are actually constructed and is able to better reason about what each table actually contains. It can answer “what’s in here” and “when can I use it” far more accurately than from warehouse signals alone.
We’re constantly working to improve our agent by increasing its ability to handle ambiguous questions, improving its reliability and accuracy with stronger validations, and integrating it more deeply into workflows. We believe it should blend naturally into how people already work, instead of functioning like a separate tool.
While our tooling will keep benefiting from underlying improvements in agent reasoning, validation, and self-correction, our team’s mission remains the same: seamlessly deliver fast, trustworthy data analysis across OpenAI’s data ecosystem.
Authors
Acknowledgements
Special thanks to the Data Productivity and Data Science teams, as well as to our many cross-functional users for their experimentation and feedback.

title: Knowledge-grounded large language model for personalized sports training plan generation - Scientific Reports
content:
Abstract
The growing demand for scientifically grounded and highly personalized fitness plans reveals the huge shortcomings of traditional recommender systems, which cannot overcome template-oriented methods and effectively cope with complex, dynamic user data. As a remedy for this shortcoming, this work utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) augmented with a domain-specific knowledge graph to develop LLM-SPTRec, a novel framework for intelligent sports training plan generation. This model successfully integrates multi-source heterogeneous user data and enhances the personalization and scientific validity of recommendations by grounding the LLM’s generative process in an expert-elicited Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG). Empirical results on a real-world dataset demonstrate that LLM-SPTRec surpasses traditional baselines—including collaborative filtering, sequential models, and general-purpose LLMs—on fundamental measures of plan coherence, goal relevance, and predicted user satisfaction. The findings of this research provide a new paradigm for the discipline of intelligent health by bridging the gap between big data analysis and expert knowledge in addition to providing a new direction for the overall field of applied AI by demonstrating that knowledge-based LLMs are capable of generating safe, effective, and scientific personal health recommendations.
Similar content being viewed by others
Introduction
The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a major paradigm shift for artificial intelligence, whose sophisticated capabilities are having a profound influence on a broad range of scientific and industrial fields. As Kumar (2024) looked around, such models have set new technical standards and are mapping the future direction of AI development1. One key part of their extreme capability is their sophisticated capacity for processing, comprehending, and generating rich, human-like language. This has opened new horizons for creating extremely intelligent and adaptive user interfaces, leading some, e.g., Agüera y Arcas (2022), to argue that the complex statistical learning contained within LLMs is an actual kind of understanding2. Recent developments in big data streams and quantum-inspired optimization have significantly enhanced real-time data analytics3. Furthermore, the convergence of machine learning and digital twin technologies has demonstrated the power of data-driven decision-making in manufacturing and health management4. Among the domains undergoing this revolution, recommender systems (RecSys) is a very promising one. Integration of LLMs is inducing a qualitative shift in recommendation models towards more complex, interactive, and human-centric designs, a trend identified in comprehensive reviews by Fan et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2025)5,6.
Recommender systems have conventionally been grounded on paradigms such as collaborative filtering and content-based analysis. While helpful to some degree, they are prone to encounter dramatic failures, notably data paucity and the “cold-start” problem, where the system struggles to recommend for new customers or items. LLMs inherently address such well-established challenges. As demonstrated through comparative research by Elmoghazy et al. (2025) and analyzed by Wu et al. (2023), the abundant world knowledge and advanced semantic understanding included in LLMs allow them to produce high-quality user and item representations from text information7,8. This capability allows for the delivery of significant and comprehensive recommendations even if user-item interaction data are limited. For instance, Lin et al. (2024) has proved in a study that LLMs can make recommender systems extremely sample-efficient9. The role of LLMs in this pursuit has thus evolved at an increasingly rapid rate. In the place of use to improve baseline models, now they are more and more coming forward as the central component of the recommendation pipeline, as a path trace set by Lin et al. (2023) in their extensive survey10. Modern approaches nowadays employ LLMs for various complex tasks. Zhang et al. (2023) developed a model where recommendations are generated by following natural language instructions, while Huang et al. (2023) developed conversational AI agents for recommendations11,12. Apart from direct proposals, Shi et al. (2024) have demonstrated that LLMs are viable learnable planners for sequential recommendations of great duration13.
This rapid development has prompted the development of a new generation of LLM-native recommendation models. Researchers are currently exploring a broad spectrum of architectures. Some approaches, as discussed by Li et al. (2023), seek to leverage LLMs to generate directly the recommended item lists in a generative way14. Others, such as the device-cloud collaborative framework proposed by Lv et al. (2025), seek hybrid solutions that capitalize on the high reasoning of cloud-based LLMs and on-device compactness of efficiency-focused recommendation models15. This movement has brought novel approaches as well to bolster the strength of such systems. For example, to promote transparency and credibility, Wang et al. (2023) developed a method for enhancing recommender systems with reasoning graphs constructed by LLM to explain the rationale of a recommendation16. To improve performance, Zhang et al. (2023) explored the use of collaborative embeddings in LLMs, while Yin et al. (2023) proposed a method for integrating heterogeneous knowledge sources17,18. As summarized by Bao et al. (2024), these cumulative advancements demonstrate a clear and compelling trend towards more intelligent, adaptive, and efficient recommender systems19.
Against this dynamic backdrop, the domain of sports science and individual welfare emerges as a particularly intriguing and high-impact application domain. As Ding (2025) observes, what is emerging is the demand for training programs that are not only tailored but also science-driven and dynamically adaptive to a given individual’s evolving fitness levels and goals20. The potential of LLMs in other similar health and well-being applications has already been demonstrated. For example, a proof-of-concept trial by Ahmed et al. (2025) employed LLMs and wearable data to enhance the well-being of students, while Alhozali (2025) employed them for customized diabetes management21,22. In a review of prospects in sport science, Connor & O’Neill (2023) highlighted the potential for LLMs to advise practitioners and athletes with customized guidance23. Such a trend has been consistent with the effective application of LLMs in other controlled environments, such as individualized learning, where Ma & Wu (2025) developed a recommendation system for providing individualized learning materials24.
Nevertheless, direct application of general-purpose LLM to sports training plan generation is fraught with serious and unique issues. Compared with recommending consumer products or media, the prescription of exercise entails inherent health risks and demands a very high degree of scientific accuracy, safety, and individualization from multidimensional physiological data. General LLMs, as they are trained on general web data, lack validated, domain-specific knowledge to ensure that a proposed plan is safe and effective. Such a “knowledge gap” is a serious issue echoed in the broader community of medical AI. A systematic review by Shool et al. (2025) and a commentary by Freyer et al. (2024) also both emphasize the utmost importance of developing solid evaluation frameworks and regulatory standards to prevent the risks of LLM deployment in health-related applications25,26. Furthermore, building an optimal training plan is actually a constrained optimization problem. As Ishii & Higuchi (2025) have examined in their paper, this requires the identification and control of numerous dependent variables, a rich reasoning task which generic models do not inherently possess the capability to deal with27.
To bridge this critical deficiency, we introduce LLM-SPTRec, a framework focusing on three core technical advances: (i) knowledge-grounded generative logic via a Sports Science Knowledge Graph, (ii) multi-modal dynamic user state integration, and (iii) a closed-loop safety validation system. Our approach surpasses standard recommendation by first constructing a dynamic, multi-faceted user model from heterogeneous data sources. Crucially, our approach adds to the LLM a purpose-built Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG), which ensures the model’s logic is grounded in established scientific principles, the safety and validity of which is guaranteed for all recommendations. By framing plan recommendation as a conditional generation task, LLM-SPTRec produces structured, interpretable, and dynamically adjustable training timetables that augment user goals and physiological conditions in real-time.
Related work
Knowledge-enhanced and graph-based recommendation
A primary challenge in building effective recommender systems, particularly in niche domains, is overcoming data sparsity and ensuring that recommendations are explainable and grounded in factual knowledge. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have emerged as a powerful solution to this problem. By encoding entities and their relationships in a structured graph format, KGs provide rich auxiliary information that can be used to enhance user and item representations. The synergy between LLMs and KGs has recently become a vibrant area of research, as it promises to combine the implicit, contextual understanding of LLMs with the explicit, factual knowledge of KGs. Several recent works have demonstrated the viability of this approach. Researchers have focused on using graph structures to augment the data available to the LLM. The LLMRec framework, introduced by Wei et al. (2023), utilizes graph augmentation strategies to explicitly model relationships between items, which helps address data sparsity and improves overall recommendation performance28. In a similar vein, Chen et al. (2023) proposed LKPNR, a framework that combines an LLM with a KG to improve the semantic understanding of complex news texts, thereby enhancing personalized news recommendation accuracy29. Furthermore, Guo et al. (2024) developed LLMGR, a framework that integrates LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for session-based recommendation, leveraging the complementary strengths of LLMs in natural language understanding and GNNs in processing relational data30.
These studies collectively validate the principle of grounding LLM-based recommenders with structured knowledge. Furthermore, the exploration of spatio-temporal similarity for recommendation31 and hybrid optimization algorithms for processing big data streams32 highlights the necessity of multi-faceted data fusion in personalized systems. Our work adopts this principle by creating a specialized Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG). To better distinguish our technical contributions, Table 1 contrasts LLM-SPTRec with existing state-of-the-art frameworks.
The evolution of LLM-driven recommendation
The advent of LLMs is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of recommender systems research, moving the field beyond traditional ranking-based paradigms. A comprehensive analysis by Xu et al. (2024) further demonstrated that LLMs can function effectively as recommender systems through careful prompt engineering, with performance being influenced by factors like model scale and architecture31. Building on this generative potential, numerous sophisticated frameworks have been proposed. To optimize LLMs for recommendation tasks, Bao et al. (2023) developed TALLRec, an effective and efficient tuning framework that significantly enhances recommendation capabilities even with limited data32. In parallel, researchers have adapted LLMs to specific recommendation scenarios, such as the session-based recommendation framework LLM4SBR by Qiao et al. (2024)33, and have developed novel methods like LC-Rec by Zheng et al. (2023) to better integrate collaborative semantics into the language model’s understanding34. As the field matures, researchers are also increasingly focused on addressing the inherent challenges and risks associated with LLMs. Given that LLMs learn from vast, uncurated data, ensuring fairness is a critical concern. The CFaiRLLM framework by Deldjoo & Noia (2024) provides a more personalized and fair assessment of LLM recommender systems by considering true preference alignment35. Another significant risk is the vulnerability of these models to data poisoning attacks. To combat this, Zhang et al. (2024) developed LoRec, an innovative framework that incorporates an LLM into the defense strategy to strengthen the robustness of sequential recommender systems36. Privacy is also a paramount concern, which Carranza et al. (2023) addressed by using differentially private LLMs to generate synthetic user queries, thus protecting user data while training the recommendation model37. Our work on LLM-SPTRec is situated within this advanced research landscape, drawing inspiration from generative and planning-based paradigms while placing a primary emphasis on the challenges of safety, factual grounding, and reliability, which are critical for the sports and health domain.

The LLM-SPTRec architecture
To address the formulated problem, we propose the LLM-SPTRec framework. The architecture is composed of three main modules: (1) The Dynamic User Profiling Module, which ingests and fuses multi-source data into a unified user state representation; (2) The Knowledge-Grounded Generation Module, where an LLM, guided by a Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG), generates the training plan; and (3) The Plan Structuring and Validation Module, which parses the LLM’s output and verifies its integrity.

This module creates a rich, machine-readable representation of the user’s state by encoding and fusing heterogeneous data sources into a single, dense vector embedding \(\:{\mathbf{s}}_{u}^{\tau\:}\). The dynamic state \(\:{\mathcal{S}}_{dyn}^{\tau\:}\), comprising time-series data from wearables (e.g., Heart Rate, HRV, Sleep Score) and training logs (e.g., Exercise ID, Reps, Weight, RPE), is processed by a Transformer-based sequential encoder to capture complex temporal patterns. Experiments
Our experiments are designed to evaluate the performance and effectiveness of our proposed intelligent sports training recommendation system. The system is built upon the synergistic architecture depicted in Fig. 3. This framework’s core principle is the integration of a Large Language Model (LLM) with a comprehensive Sports Knowledge Base & User Big Data. In this model, the LLM functions as the natural language interface and personalized plan generator, while the knowledge base—containing scientific principles, an exercise database, and user-specific data (e.g., biometrics, workout logs)—provides the essential factual grounding and safety constraints. The central mechanism is a knowledge-augmented generation process: relevant, structured information is retrieved from the knowledge base to guide the LLM, ensuring that the generated plans are both highly personalized and scientifically sound. The following subsections detail the datasets, metrics, and results of experiments conducted to validate this architecture.
Experimental setup
A robust and reproducible experimental protocol is crucial for validating our claims. This section details the dataset, baseline models, evaluation metrics, and implementation specifics used throughout our evaluation.
Our experiments are conducted on a large-scale, multi-modal, real-world dataset, which we have curated and named SportFit-1 M. This dataset is an amalgamation of anonymized user data from several leading fitness applications and wearable device platforms, ensuring a diverse representation of user demographics, fitness levels, and goals. To ensure data quality, we performed rigorous preprocessing, filtering out users with fewer than 10 activity logs and those with data completeness below 50%. The resulting dataset provides a rich, longitudinal view of user behavior and physiological responses, making it an ideal testbed for evaluating adaptive recommendation systems. The key statistics of the processed SportFit-1 M dataset are summarized in Table 6. To address potential biases, we provide a demographic breakdown: the population consists of 58% male and 42% female users, with 75% aged between 18 and 45.
To benchmark the performance of LLM-SPTRec, we selected a strong and diverse set of baseline models that represent different algorithmic paradigms in recommendation systems. These include: ItemCF, a classic item-based collaborative filtering method representing traditional, non-sequential approaches; GRU4Rec, a sequential model using Gated Recurrent Units to capture temporal dynamics in user behavior; KGAT (Knowledge Graph Attention Network), a state-of-the-art knowledge-aware model that leverages a KG to enhance recommendations; and P5 (Pre-train, Personalized Prompt, and Predict Paradigm), a powerful and generic LLM-based recommendation framework that unifies various tasks into a language processing format. This selection allows for a multi-faceted comparison, evaluating LLM-SPTRec against methods that specialize in collaborative signals, sequence modeling, knowledge fusion, and general-purpose language generation, respectively.
Evaluating the quality of a generated training plan requires moving beyond traditional ranking metrics. Therefore, we designed a comprehensive evaluation protocol comprising two categories of metrics. The first, Ranking-based Metrics, assesses the accuracy of recommending individual exercise items, using standard metrics like Hit Ratio (HR@K) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@K) for K={10, 50}. The second, and more crucial, category is Plan-level Metrics, designed to evaluate the holistic quality of the entire generated plan. This includes the Plan Coherence Score (PCS), a composite score (1–5) derived from a model trained on expert ratings, which assesses the scientific soundness of the plan’s structure (e.g., muscle group rotation, progressive overload); the Goal Achievement Index (GAI), a score (0–1) calculated using a fine-tuned BERT model to measure the semantic alignment between the generated plan and the user’s stated goals; and User Satisfaction (USAT), a predicted 1–5 star rating from a simulator trained on historical user feedback, reflecting the personalization and appeal of the plan.
The LLM-SPTRec framework was implemented in PyTorch, utilizing a LLaMA-2-7B model as its generative backbone. The Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG) embeddings were learned using the RotatE model. Training was conducted in two stages: an initial Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage, followed by a Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) stage using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. All baseline models were implemented using their official codebases or the RecBole library, with hyperparameters meticulously tuned for optimal performance on our dataset. Results and analysis
The overall performance of LLM-SPTRec and all baseline models on the SportFit-1 M dataset is presented in Table 8. The results unequivocally demonstrate the comprehensive superiority of our proposed framework. LLM-SPTRec significantly outperforms all baselines across every evaluation metric, encompassing both ranking accuracy and plan-level quality. This highlights its unique ability to not only predict relevant exercises accurately but also to synthesize them into a coherent, goal-oriented, and satisfying training plan. The performance of the baselines reveals a clear hierarchy of capabilities. ItemCF, lacking any sequential or contextual understanding, performs the poorest. GRU4Rec improves upon this by modeling user sequences, while KGAT achieves further gains by incorporating domain knowledge, which is particularly beneficial for the plan-level metrics (PCS, GAI). An interesting observation arises from the performance of P5, the generic LLM framework. While it struggles with traditional ranking metrics, even underperforming KGAT, it shows strong performance on plan-level metrics, second only to LLM-SPTRec. This suggests that while general-purpose LLMs possess inherent strengths in understanding natural language goals and generating structured text, they require specialized domain knowledge and architectural enhancements to excel in both accuracy and quality for a specialized task like training plan recommendation. The success of LLM-SPTRec stems from its synergistic design, which integrates the generative power of an LLM with a dynamic user profiling module for deep personalization, a grounding knowledge graph for scientific validity, and a reinforcement learning loop for continuous optimization based on user feedback.
For facilitating the training of reinforcement learning algorithms, the raw interaction data is transformed into a trajectory format. Each trajectory is an extended sequence of experience quadruples. Specifically, a standard MDP quadruple \(\:\left[{s}_{t},{a}_{t},{r}_{t},{s}_{t+1}\right]\) is augmented to \(\:\left[{s}_{t},{a}_{t},{a}_{t}^{+},{r}_{t},{s}_{t+1}\right]\). Here, \(\:{\mathcal{I}}_{0}\) denotes an empty sequence corresponding to the initial state representation \(\:{s}_{0}\), representing a user’s entry into the recommendation system without prior interactions, which is randomly initialized. \(\:{\mathcal{I}}_{1:t}\) corresponds to \(\:{s}_{t}\), representing the user’s interaction sequence at time \(\:t\). The action \(\:{a}_{t}\) denotes the item \(\:{i}_{t+1}\) that the user truly interacted with in the recorded dataset at time \(\:t+1\). Crucially, \(\:{a}_{t}^{+}\)represents the next “high-value” item that the user interacted with after time \(\:t\) in the dataset. The reward \(\:{r}_{t}\) is the instantaneous reward received by the agent after taking action \(\:{a}_{t}\), which is manually assigned based on the user’s actual rating for the item. In the context of supervised learning methods, \(\:{a}_{t}^{+}\)serves as the target label, with the interaction sequence \(\:{\mathcal{I}}_{1:t}\) as input, and the optimization objective being to enhance the accuracy of label prediction.
To provide a more intuitive visualization of these performance gaps, particularly on the crucial plan-level metrics, Fig. 4 plots the comparison of PCS, GAI, and USAT scores across the top-performing models. The chart clearly illustrates that while knowledge-aware models like KGAT and generative models like P5 show competence in some aspects, LLM-SPTRec establishes a commanding lead across all three dimensions of plan quality. Its significantly higher scores in coherence (PCS), goal alignment (GAI), and user satisfaction (USAT) visually affirm the effectiveness of its integrated architecture.
To validate the necessity of each key component within the LLM-SPTRec architecture, we conducted a thorough ablation study. We created three variants of our model by removing one critical component at a time: (1) w/o KG, which removes the guidance from the Sports Science Knowledge Graph; (2) w/o RLHF, which omits the reinforcement learning optimization stage and relies solely on supervised fine-tuning; and (3) w/o Dyn-Profile, which operates using only the user’s static profile and goals, ignoring all dynamic physiological and behavioral data. The results, summarized in Table 9, demonstrate the significant and distinct contribution of each ablated component. The removal of the knowledge graph (w/o KG) causes the most substantial drop in the Plan Coherence Score (PCS), confirming that the SSKG is the bedrock of the model’s ability to generate scientifically valid and safe plans. Without it, the LLM is prone to “hallucinating” unsafe or illogical exercise combinations. The absence of reinforcement learning (w/o RLHF) leads to the largest decrease in User Satisfaction (USAT), indicating that while SFT can teach the model to mimic expert plans, only RLHF allows it to truly adapt to individual user preferences and feedback, thereby maximizing satisfaction. Finally, removing the dynamic user profile (w/o Dyn-Profile) significantly impairs both the Goal Achievement Index (GAI) and USAT, proving that real-time physiological and performance data is essential for creating truly personalized and adaptive plans that respond to the user’s current state. Collectively, these findings affirm that all three components are integral and work synergistically to achieve the framework’s state-of-the-art performance.
Figure 5 visually summarizes the impact of removing each component on the three core plan-level metrics. The chart makes the performance degradation strikingly clear. For instance, the removal of the knowledge graph (w/o KG) results in a dramatic drop in the Plan Coherence Score (PCS), visually confirming its role as the scientific backbone of the model. Similarly, the absence of reinforcement learning (w/o RLHF) leads to the most significant decrease in User Satisfaction (USAT), highlighting the importance of personal feedback optimization. This graphical representation underscores the synergistic necessity of each module for generating high-quality, scientifically sound, and personalized training plans.
We conducted a human evaluation involving five certified trainers to rate the “Safety” and “Feasibility” of 100 random plans. LLM-SPTRec achieved a safety score of 4.8/5.0, compared to 3.1/5.0 for a general LLM (LLaMA-2). The inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen’s kappa was 0.76. Case studies revealed that while general LLMs often neglect recovery periods, LLM-SPTRec correctly identifies overtraining risks through its KG constraints.
Conclusion
We have successfully addressed the complex issue of creating personalized, science-driven, and dynamically adaptive sport training plans. The research melted away into creating and validating LLM-SPTRec, a new solution specifically designed to tackle difficulties posed by heterogeneous user data, intricate exercise science principles, and dynamic nature of personal fitness journeys. The innovation of LLM-SPTRec is in its synergistic design by intentionally combining dynamic multi-modal user profiling, an anchoring-relevant domain-specific Sports Science Knowledge Graph (SSKG), and the state-of-the-art reasoning and generative power of Large Language Models (LLMs). This was accomplished by modeling the holistic user state from behavioral and physiological data streams, guiding and constraining the generation process using the SSKG, and applying a two-stage optimization protocol of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from user rating to render the generated plans satisfying and effective. Large-scale experimental evaluation on the SportFit-1 M dataset highly confirmed the better performance of LLM-SPTRec. The results consistently demonstrated that not only does our system improve upon recommending single exercises, but more importantly, it has better plans overall, as evidenced by significantly higher coherence, goal congruence, and user satisfaction scores than sequential, knowledge-aware, and generic LLM-based baselines.
Our contribution is not another algorithm. It provides a powerful and versatile tool that effectively bridges the gap between individual big data richness and leveraging expert domain knowledge, making it particularly well-suited for high-consequence applications where safety and scientific validity are paramount. The successful grounding of the LLM using a knowledge graph illustrates the potential of this approach to decrease factual “hallucinations” and increase the reliability of generative AI in professional applications. The study provides forward-looking direction for researchers and practitioners who seek to develop the next generation of intelligent coaching and personalized health systems. In the long term, the promising findings of LLM-SPTRec create a range of possibilities for future research. These include expanding the SSKG to even more general concepts such as nutrition and injury rehabilitation routines, extending the framework to other health domains such as mental well-being and meal planning, and integrating richer modalities such as video-based video exercise form analysis to facilitate even more comprehensive and interactive coaching experiences.
